documents.title: Winning the Race: America's AI Action Plan
documents.implementation_notes: Published July 2025 pursuant to EO 14179 by APST Michael J. Kratsios, Special Advisor David O. Sacks, and APNSA Marco A. Rubio. Sets out over 90 recommended federal policy actions across three pillars: (I) Accelerate AI Innovation (deregulation, revising NIST AI RMF, supporting open-weight models, regulatory sandboxes, worker retraining/AI Workforce Research Hub, science/datasets, evaluations, federal/DOD adoption, legal deepfake forensics); (II) Build American AI Infrastructure (NEPA/FAST-41/CWA permitting reform, grid expansion, semiconductor reshoring, high-security military data centers, skilled trades apprenticeships, AI-ISAC, CISA AI incident playbooks); and (III) Lead in International AI Diplomacy and Security (full-stack AI exports, countering China in standards bodies, chip location verification and sub-system export controls, CAISI frontier CBRNE/cyber evaluations, enforceable biosecurity synthesis screening).
documents.framing_rationale_summary: America's AI Action Plan is dominantly framed around economic_competitiveness, organizing all three pillars around 'winning the race' to achieve global AI dominance, exporting the full U.S. AI technology stack worldwide, reshoring semiconductor manufacturing, and ushering in an industrial revolution. Economic_competitiveness narrowly edges out national_security because global ecosystem leadership, market-standard setting, and industrial buildout frame both domestic deregulation and international alliances. National_security is a close runner-up (military preeminence, China rivalry, chip export controls, critical-infrastructure defense), paired with strong innovation_enablement (deregulation, permitting reform, sandboxes, open-weight support), an explicit labor_transition agenda (AI Workforce Research Hub, DOL rapid retraining for displaced workers, skilled-trades apprenticeships), and existential_catastrophic rationales for CAISI frontier CBRNE/cyber evaluations and nucleic-acid biosecurity screening.

documents.title: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights
documents.implementation_notes: Non-binding White House OSTP white paper and Technical Companion ('From Principles to Practice') published October 4, 2022 (retained as a historical baseline in U.S. AI governance). Articulates five rights-protective principles—Safe and Effective Systems; Algorithmic Discrimination Protections; Data Privacy; Notice and Explanation; and Human Alternatives, Consideration, and Fallback—scoped to automated systems meaningfully impacting rights, opportunities, or access to critical resources/services, with heightened protections for sensitive domains (health, employment, education, criminal justice, personal finance, youth) and carve-outs for national security, defense, and law enforcement equities. Imposes no binding compliance obligations or legal remedies.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights is overwhelmingly framed around fundamental_rights: its stated purpose is to protect civil rights, civil liberties, personal-data privacy, non-discrimination, equity for underserved communities, human dignity, and democratic values against harms from automated systems. Fundamental_rights decisively leads consumer_public_safety, which serves as the main secondary frame via protections against unsafe clinical tools, stalking devices, non-consensual intimate imagery, and defective automated systems. Labor_transition (workplace surveillance chilling union organizing, automated firing without recourse, algorithmic quotas/bonuses) and innovation_enablement ('clear rules of the road that allow new ideas to flourish') appear as distinct supporting frames, alongside minor social_stability (trust and democratic process) and national_security (disclaimer carve-out) mentions.

documents.title: AI Congressional Mandates, Executive Orders and Actions | NIST
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Official NIST reference page (initial publication 2025-01-21, subsequently updated through at least 2025-07-23) cataloging the congressional statutes (CHIPS and Science Act of 2022, National AI Initiative Act of 2020), America's AI Action Plan (July 2025), and Executive Orders (Jan 2025 EO 14179, rescinded Oct 2023 EO 14110, Dec 2020 EO 13960, Feb 2019 EO 13859) driving NIST's non-regulatory AI standards, testbed, cybersecurity, and evaluation activities. As a summary webpage, it imposes no direct legal obligations or enforcement mechanisms.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: This mandates catalog reflects a close three-way balance led by innovation_enablement, which runs across every cited statute and executive action via technical standards, testbeds, research infrastructure (NAIRR), open-source/open-weight encouragement, AI adoption, and reviewing regulatory obstacles from rescinded EO 14110. Innovation_enablement narrowly edges out national_security and economic_competitiveness, which are strongly articulated in the 2025 executive actions through military/intelligence data centers, critical infrastructure cybersecurity, biosecurity, frontier national security risk evaluations, and sustaining America's global AI dominance. Fundamental_rights (free speech, testing for bias in training data) and consumer_public_safety (safe and trustworthy AI) appear as smaller supporting rationales.

documents.title: AI Risk Management Framework - Engage | NIST
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Administrative stakeholder-engagement webpage for the NIST AI RMF (originally published 2021-07-13 and updated through the January 26, 2023 launch of AI RMF 1.0). Summarizes NIST's workshops, RFI, draft consultations, and ongoing feedback mechanisms for revising the voluntary Framework, Playbook, Roadmap, and Crosswalks; contains no operative safety requirements or enforcement hooks.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: This procedural engagement page contains modest framing language led by innovation_enablement, emphasizing a voluntary, consensus-driven, collaborative standards-development process that adapts complementary guidance based on real-world practitioner experience. Fundamental_rights (inclusion of civil society and a workshop on Bias in AI), consumer_public_safety (consumer stakeholders), and economic_competitiveness (AI and the Economy conference) appear only as minor contextual signals.

documents.title: AI Risk Management Framework FAQs | NIST
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Official NIST AI RMF FAQ companion page (initial publication 2021-07-13, updated through the January 26, 2023 AI RMF 1.0 release). Clarifies the Framework's voluntary non-binding status, broad scalability across public and private sectors, seven trustworthiness characteristics and their tradeoffs, development timeline (2021 RFI through Jan 2023 launch), and relationship to the companion Playbook and other NIST frameworks.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The AI RMF FAQs are dominantly framed around innovation_enablement, presenting a voluntary, scalable, non-mandatory standards framework aimed at fostering innovative approaches to trustworthiness, improving measurement science, and building confidence in AI systems. Innovation_enablement leads consumer_public_safety, which is a strong runner-up focused on managing AI risks to individuals, organizations, society, and quality of life through safe, valid, and reliable systems. Economic_competitiveness ('enhance economic security') and fundamental_rights ('privacy-enhanced, and fair with harmful bias managed') serve as clear secondary frames, with a minor national_security nod to NSCAI recommendations.

documents.title: AI Risk Management Framework: Initial Draft - March 17, 2022
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Superseded consultation draft of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework published March 17, 2022 (public comment deadline April 29, 2022; later superseded by the August 18, 2022 Second Draft and January 26, 2023 AI RMF 1.0). Organizes trustworthiness into a three-class taxonomy (technical characteristics, socio-technical characteristics, guiding principles) and introduces the four Core functions (Map, Measure, Manage, Govern). Explicitly voluntary, outcome-focused, non-prescriptive, law- and regulation-agnostic, and defers Profiles, Effectiveness, and the companion Practice Guide to subsequent drafts.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The AI RMF Initial Draft is dominantly framed around innovation_enablement, positioning a voluntary, flexible, non-prescriptive risk management framework as the vehicle to cultivate trust, create opportunities for innovation, and enable widespread acceptance and realization of AI's full potential. Innovation_enablement narrowly edges out consumer_public_safety, which is a strong runner-up emphasizing minimizing operational failures, physical safety hazards (e.g., factories and roads), and adverse impacts on individuals, organizations, and society. Fundamental_rights is a prominent third frame, anchored in civil liberties and rights, human autonomy and dignity in privacy, anti-discrimination, fairness, and actionable redress.

documents.title: AI Risk Management Framework: Second Draft - August 18, 2022
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Second public consultation draft of the NIST AI RMF released August 18, 2022 (public comment deadline September 29, 2022; supersedes the March 17, 2022 Initial Draft and later superseded by AI RMF 1.0 on January 26, 2023). Consolidates trustworthiness into seven characteristics, adds a dedicated Human Factors discussion, expands the Core into full coded GOVERN 1–6, MAP 1–5, MEASURE 1–4, and MANAGE 1–4 subcategories, introduces Use-Case and Temporal Profiles, and adds Appendix A (AI Actor Tasks) and Appendix B (How AI Risks Differ from Traditional Software Risks).
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The AI RMF Second Draft is dominantly framed around innovation_enablement, explicitly elevating 'pro-innovation' alongside risk-based, resource-efficient, voluntary, and non-prescriptive attributes to cultivate trust and realize AI's full potential without rigid compliance checklists. Innovation_enablement narrowly leads consumer_public_safety, which is a strong runner-up centered on preventing physical, psychological, property, and operational harms across the lifecycle (including safely ceasing deployment when severe harms occur). Fundamental_rights is a substantial third frame grounded in preserving civil liberties and rights, safeguarding human autonomy and dignity through privacy, and curbing algorithmic bias and discrimination, with minor mentions of catastrophic risks and economic/national security context.

documents.title: AI Standards | NIST
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Official NIST ITL AI Program standards page (originally published 2021-08-03 and updated through March 6, 2026). Describes NIST's non-regulatory standards strategy: the AI Standards Zero Drafts pilot, A Plan for Global Engagement on AI Standards (NIST AI 100-5e2025, July 26, 2024), federal interagency coordination via ICSP/AISCWG, alignment of AI RMF 1.0 with international ISO/IEC standards and crosswalks, and GCR-26-069 (Jan 15, 2026) on evaluating AI standards development.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The page is overwhelmingly framed around innovation_enablement, arguing that stakeholder-driven voluntary consensus standards, zero-draft pilots, and international RMF alignment accelerate standards creation, unleash AI innovation, and foster trustworthy AI adoption ecosystems. Innovation_enablement clearly edges out economic_competitiveness, which appears as a secondary rationale via alignment with the National Standards Strategy for Critical and Emerging Technology and U.S. Leadership in AI plan. Social_stability (public trust) and consumer_public_safety (managing AI risks for trustworthy development and use) play supporting roles.

documents.title: BIS Final Rule: Revision to License Review Policy for Advanced Computing Commodities (91 FR 1684)
documents.issuing_body: U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS)
documents.implementation_notes: Published and effective January 15, 2026 (91 FR 1684, Docket No. 260112-0028, RIN 0694-AK43), this BIS final rule amends 15 CFR §§ 742.6, 744.23, 748.8, and Supplement No. 2 to Part 748 (adding paragraph (dd)) to shift U.S. export license review for commercially available mid-tier advanced AI chips (TPP < 21,000 and total DRAM bandwidth < 6,500 GB/s, such as NVIDIA H200 and AMD MI325X) destined to China and Macau from a presumption of denial to case-by-case review. Eligibility requires nine binding certifications: U.S. supply sufficiency and zero global foundry-capacity diversion, a 50% cap relative to aggregate TPP shipped to U.S. commercial customers, prohibition of military/military-intelligence/WMD/part-744 end uses and remote access, consignee KYC and physical security disclosures, IaaS remote end-user reporting across eight countries of concern, IaaS restrictions barring unauthorized transfers of trained model weights or remote access to trained algorithms, and pre-export independent U.S. third-party testing lab verification.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: This BIS final rule is dominantly framed around national security, justifying its tightly conditioned case-by-case export licensing policy as necessary to protect U.S. national security and foreign policy interests, preserve U.S. technological superiority, prevent military and military-intelligence end uses or unauthorized remote access, and ensure destination countries do not exceed U.S. compute capabilities—explicitly noting exemption from E.O. 14192 because its primary direct benefit is improving national security. Economic competitiveness forms a clear secondary frame through provisions safeguarding U.S. leadership in AI, preventing delays to U.S. commercial customer chip orders, blocking diversion of global foundry capacity away from U.S. end users, and capping China and Macau exports at 50 percent of aggregate U.S. commercial shipments. A minor existential and catastrophic risk element appears in the mandatory certification screening out nuclear, missile, chemical, and biological weapons end uses and end users.

documents.title: BIS Rule: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors (91 FR 74970)
documents.issuing_body: U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS)
documents.implementation_notes: Published and effective November 19, 2026 (91 FR 74970, Docket No. 261116-0005, RIN 0694-AK50; using 'Super Intelligence (SI)' terminology pursuant to EO 14434), this sweeping BIS Interim Final Rule establishes four major pillars: (1) new 15 CFR § 744.24 prohibiting unlicensed exports, reexports, or transfers of advanced AI semiconductors to overseas data centers worldwide providing >12,000,000 aggregate TPP (including across physically or digitally linked data centers) to Country Group D:5 or Macau companies, backed by KYC ownership due diligence, no de minimis relief, mandatory recipient end-use notices, and a narrow commercial-recommender-system exclusion (explicitly excluding generative models); (2) new diversion-risk destination license requirements for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil, and Thailand (§ 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A)(1)), excluding U.S.-headquartered entities subject to monthly § 743.10 reporting; (3) tighter front-end fabricator/OSAT presumptions under ECCN 3A090.a Note 1 and § 744.23(a)(3)(i)(C); and (4) formal rescission of the January 2025 Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule—eliminating ECCN 4E091 AI model-weights controls, the model-weights FDP rule, country tiers, Data Center VEU authorizations, and License Exceptions AIA and LPP while retaining License Exception ACM and worldwide advanced-computing FDP jurisdiction under § 734.9(h).
documents.framing_rationale_summary: This BIS interim final rule is predominantly framed around national security, seeking to stop foreign adversaries headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau from circumventing U.S. chip export controls via overseas cloud data centers and third-country diversion hubs to train advanced AI ('Super Intelligence') models supporting military and intelligence activities, cyber-espionage, algorithmic theft, and shifts in global military balances of power—invoking an E.O. 14192 national-security exemption. Existential and catastrophic risk forms a prominent secondary rationale because BIS explicitly anchors the 12,000,000 aggregate TPP remote-compute threshold in preventing foreign actors from accelerating development of weapons of mass destruction and executing sophisticated zero-day cyberattacks against critical infrastructure. A targeted innovation enablement layer appears in formally rescinding the AI Diffusion Rule's worldwide license requirements and country tiers to streamline licensing, retaining License Exception ACM to support allied supply chains, and exempting commercial recommender systems and U.S.-headquartered firms from unnecessary licensing friction.

documents.title: Chatbots in consumer finance
documents.implementation_notes: Published June 2023 as a CFPB research Issue Spotlight examining rule-based and LLM/generative AI chatbots across U.S. consumer finance (including all top 10 commercial banks). Analyzes consumer complaints documenting 'doom loops', unrecognized disputes, factual hallucinations, blocked human offramps, system downtime, impersonation/phishing scams, chat-log data security risks, and training-data privacy leakage, while encouraging consumer complaints and industry whistleblower tips alongside active CFPB market monitoring.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: CFPB's Issue Spotlight on Chatbots in Consumer Finance is dominantly framed around consumer_public_safety, centering on concrete financial harms to consumers—including junk fees, late fees, default, unresolved transaction disputes, inaccurate financial information, 'doom loops', phishing/impersonation scams, and eroded customer trust when institutions replace live human support with deficient chatbots. Consumer_public_safety strongly outweighs fundamental_rights because the report's primary evidence and risk taxonomy focus on operational service failures and consumer financial injury. Fundamental_rights serves as a substantive secondary frame covering consumer data privacy, PII breaches in chat logs and training datasets, disproportionate barriers for limited-English-proficiency users, algorithmic bias, and invoking federal legal rights, with a minor economic_competitiveness note on weak market competition and lock-in.

documents.title: Consumer Financial Protection Circular 2022-03: Adverse action notification requirements in connection with credit decisions based on complex algorithms
documents.implementation_notes: Issued May 26, 2022 as an APA general statement of policy (5 U.S.C. 553(b)) promoting enforcement consistency across federal and state consumer financial enforcers. Confirms that ECOA and Regulation B written adverse action notice duties apply equally regardless of model complexity, that disclosing FCRA credit-score factors or generic sample checklist reasons does not satisfy ECOA unless they reflect the actual principal factors scored, and that creditors using post-hoc explanation methods must validate the accuracy of those approximations.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: CFPB Circular 2022-03 is dominantly framed around fundamental_rights, grounding adverse action explainability mandates in the Equal Credit Opportunity Act's anti-discrimination protections across protected classes and procedural fairness enabling applicants to detect and challenge credit errors. Fundamental_rights narrowly edges out consumer_public_safety because preventing discrimination ex ante is highlighted as the core statutory purpose of ECOA's notice rule. Consumer_public_safety is a very strong runner-up, explicitly invoking ECOA's 'twin goals of consumer protection and education' and the CFPB's mandate against unfair, deceptive, and abusive practices, while economic_competitiveness plays a minor supporting role via Congress's view that notice rules have a beneficial competitive effect on the credit marketplace.

documents.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability
documents.implementation_notes: Part 2 of the U.S. Copyright Office's multi-part report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, released January 29, 2025 following the August 2023 Notice of Inquiry (over 10,000 public comments). Reaffirms that U.S. copyright requires human authorship under the Copyright Clause and Title 17, distinguishes assistive AI uses (fully protectable) from generative AI outputs lacking sufficient human expressive control, concludes that prompts alone—even detailed or iteratively revised prompts—do not confer authorship under current technology, confirms protection for perceptible human expressive inputs and creative selection/arrangement/modification of AI outputs on a case-by-case basis, surveys international approaches (South Korea, Japan, China, EU, UK, Canada, Australia), and rejects creating new copyright or sui generis protection for purely AI-generated works. To be operationalized via updated registration guidance and revisions to the Compendium of U.S. Copyright Office Practices.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The Copyright Office's copyrightability report is dominantly framed around fundamental rights, anchoring U.S. AI copyright policy in constitutional Copyright Clause principles, free expression, human-centered authorship, and empowering creators—including creators with disabilities—to realize their own creative expression rather than departing from constitutional principles for foreign competition. Labor and workforce transition serves as a major secondary frame: the Office explicitly warns against granting copyright or sui generis protection to purely AI-generated outputs because an oversupply of rapidly generated synthetic content risks diluting royalties, displacing creative professions, and undermining human authors' ability to make a living from their craft. Innovation enablement is a strong supporting frame, emphasizing that existing copyright law adapts flexibly to new technology, protects assistive AI tool use without friction, and preserves ample development incentives without premature statutory disruption.

documents.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3: Generative AI Training
documents.implementation_notes: Pre-publication version of Part 3 of the U.S. Copyright Office's Report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, issued May 9, 2025 following over 10,000 Notice of Inquiry comments. Analyzes prima facie reproduction and derivative-work infringement across dataset curation, model training, memorized model weights, RAG, and outputs; provides a four-factor Section 107 fair use framework distinguishing transformative noncommercial research and guarded non-substitutive deployments from commercial expressive market substitution, market dilution (including stylistic imitation), and pirated/unlawful dataset access; surveys EU, Japan, Singapore, UK, Israel, South Korea, China, Brazil, and Spain approaches; rejects compulsory licensing and mandatory opt-outs at this stage; encourages DOJ antitrust clarity for collective licensing; and recommends allowing voluntary direct and collective licensing markets to mature with extended collective licensing (ECL) reserved for demonstrated sector-specific market failures.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The Copyright Office's generative AI training report is dominantly framed around innovation enablement, arguing that flexible fair-use doctrine and non-interventionist, market-led voluntary licensing best allow transformative AI innovation and practical licensing ecosystems to flourish without locking in rigid compulsory statutes. Fundamental rights is a strong secondary frame grounded in authors' exclusive statutory property rights, lawful access control, and consent principles—leading the Office to reject mandatory opt-outs and compulsory derogations of authorial rights. Labor and workforce transition carries substantial weight as the Office highlights unprecedented market dilution, royalty dilution, and stylistic imitation threatening creative professionals' livelihoods and incentives to keep creating. Economic competitiveness forms a distinct secondary pillar, explicitly tying balanced copyright and licensing solutions—and fair use for analytical and research deployments—to sustaining American global leadership across both its world-class technology and creative industries.

documents.title: Crosswalks to the NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) | NIST
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Companion NIST webpage introducing crosswalks mapping AI RMF 1.0 to external AI standards and governance frameworks. Reaffirms the AI RMF's voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific, and use-case-agnostic design under P.L. 116-283 and invites public comments on crosswalks.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: This brief companion page is dominantly framed around innovation_enablement, emphasizing a voluntary, flexible, non-sector-specific, internationally aligned standards resource designed to equip AI actors to increase system trustworthiness without prescriptive mandates. Innovation_enablement edges out fundamental_rights (signaled explicitly by 'rights-preserving') and consumer_public_safety (managing the many risks of AI to promote responsible use), both of which appear as concise supporting rationales.

documents.title: DoD Directive 3000.09: Autonomy in Weapon Systems
documents.implementation_notes: Approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks and effective January 25, 2023, DoD Directive 3000.09 reissues and cancels the 2012 directive to modernize U.S. defense governance for AI-enabled autonomous and semi-autonomous weapon systems. It binds all DoD components to design systems enabling appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force; enforce temporal, geographic, and operational engagement bounds with automatic termination or operator re-authorization; execute rigorous hardware/software V&V, iterative cyber T&E, emergent-behavior analysis, rapid-reprogramming validation, and post-IOT&E regression testing; comply with DoDI 8500.01 cybersecurity, MIL-STD-882E system safety, the law of war, and the five DoD AI Ethical Principles (Responsible, Equitable, Traceable, Reliable, Governable); and route covered autonomous weapon systems through dual-gate senior review (pre-development and pre-fielding) supported by a permanent Autonomous Weapon Systems Working Group.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: DoD Directive 3000.09 is dominantly framed around national security, governing the acquisition, resilience, warfighter readiness, and operational deployment of autonomous and semi-autonomous military weapon systems against adaptive adversaries in contested cyberspace while explicitly balancing risk reduction with meeting mission objectives and preserving urgent-military-need waivers. Consumer and public safety serves as a major secondary rationale centered on operational weapon safety, preventing unintended engagements, protecting non-targets, minimizing failure probabilities and collateral damage, and avoiding unintended death, injury, or property and environmental harm. Fundamental rights provides an important secondary legal and ethical frame anchored in strict compliance with the law of war, international treaties, rules of engagement, human judgment over the use of force, and the DoD AI Ethical Principles requiring responsible, equitable, bias-minimized, traceable, and governable AI capabilities.

documents.title: Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence
documents.implementation_notes: Signed January 23, 2025, EO 14179 resets federal AI policy by revoking barriers stemming from the revoked EO 14110 of October 30, 2023. It directs an immediate interagency review to suspend, revise, rescind, or grant exemptions from EO 14110-derived agency actions, orders OMB to revise Memoranda M-24-10 and M-24-18 within 60 days, and mandates an AI Action Plan within 180 days. It imposes no private-sector technical safety controls or coercive external enforcement mechanisms.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: EO 14179 is dominantly framed around economic_competitiveness, anchoring federal policy in sustaining and enhancing America's global AI dominance, free-market strength, and global leadership. Economic_competitiveness edges out innovation_enablement because removing regulatory barriers is explicitly subordinated to the overarching zero-sum strategic objective of retaining global AI leadership and dominance. Innovation_enablement is a major secondary frame via the revocation of prior policies deemed obstacles to entrepreneurial AI innovation, while national_security appears explicitly in the Section 2 policy mandate and APNSA co-leadership, alongside a brief anti-ideological-bias rationale.

documents.title: Executive Order 14365: Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (90 FR 58499)
documents.implementation_notes: Signed December 11, 2025 and published December 16, 2025 (90 FR 58499). Rather than establishing technical AI safety requirements on private entities, EO 14365 targets State-level AI regulatory fragmentation via DOJ litigation, Commerce evaluation, BEAD and discretionary grant funding restrictions, FCC preemption inquiry, FTC UDAP preemption policy, and a federal legislative recommendation that expressly preserves lawful State laws on child safety, compute/data center infrastructure, and State government procurement/use of AI.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: EO 14365 is dominantly framed around economic_competitiveness, justifying federal preemption of State AI statutes as essential to sustain global AI dominance, attract trillions of dollars in investment, and win the AI race. Economic_competitiveness narrowly edges out innovation_enablement because removing the 50-state compliance patchwork and burdensome regulation is explicitly framed as the means to achieve global supremacy against foreign adversaries. Innovation_enablement is a close secondary frame emphasizing start-up compliance relief and a minimally burdensome national standard, accompanied by national_security (explicit race with adversaries for supremacy), and secondary references to fundamental_rights (First Amendment and anti-censorship) and consumer_public_safety (child safety protections).

documents.title: Executive Order 14409: Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security (91 FR 34565)
documents.implementation_notes: Signed June 2, 2026 and published June 5, 2026 (91 FR 34565). Pairs mandatory federal agency cyber-defense hardening (via CNSS, Department of War, and CISA Binding Operational Directives) and prioritized DOJ criminal enforcement against malicious AI/agent cyber intrusions with voluntary private-sector collaboration—specifically an AI cybersecurity clearinghouse and an NSA-led classified frontier cyber capability benchmark with voluntary up-to-30-day pre-release government access for covered frontier models, while explicitly rejecting mandatory model licensing.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: EO 14409 is dominantly framed around national_security, centering on new national-security considerations from advanced AI cyber capabilities, protecting American intellectual property from adversaries, defending National Security Systems and Department of War IT, and running an NSA-led classified frontier cyber benchmark. National_security edges out innovation_enablement because nearly every operative section deploys defense, intelligence, and homeland-security authorities to harden systems and confront external threats. Innovation_enablement is a prominent secondary frame—rejecting burdensome regulation and mandatory licensing in favor of voluntary industry collaboration and early trusted-partner access—supported by economic_competitiveness (global AI dominance and investment) and consumer_public_safety (defending rural hospitals, community banks, local utilities, and prosecuting cybercrime).

documents.title: Executive Order 14434: Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence (91 FR 63129)
documents.implementation_notes: Signed September 29, 2026 (filed in the Federal Register on October 1, 2026, and published at 91 FR 63129 on October 2, 2026). Directs executive departments and agencies, to the maximum extent permitted by law, to use 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' instead of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents, and not to acknowledge the usage of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in applicable settings. Does not require altering previously issued regulations, Presidential actions, contracts, grants, or other historical documents. Adopts the existing statutory definition of 'artificial intelligence' in 15 U.S.C. 9401(3) on an interim basis unless superseded by subsequent Presidential action or Act of Congress. Subject to applicable law and availability of appropriations, and creates no legally enforceable rights or benefits.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: Executive Order 14434 justifies replacing 'Artificial Intelligence' with 'Super Intelligence' primarily through an innovation_enablement frame, emphasizing the transformative capabilities, human ingenuity, creativity, scientific and medical breakthroughs, and limitless opportunities created by frontier technologies. Economic_competitiveness is a prominent secondary frame, reflected in references to America standing at the forefront of a technological revolution, world-leading companies, and entrepreneurial spirit; however, innovation_enablement edges it out because the order focuses on celebrating technological promise and scientific advancement rather than framing policy around GDP growth, trade advantage, or zero-sum international economic rivalry. No national security, fundamental rights, consumer safety, social stability, labor transition, or catastrophic risk rationales are invoked.

documents.title: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions
documents.implementation_notes: Final FDA guidance originally issued December 4, 2024 and updated August 18, 2025 implementing FD&C Act Section 515C (enacted by FDORA, Pub. L. 117-328). Applies to manual and automatically implemented ('continuous learning') modifications to AI-enabled Device Software Functions (AI-DSFs) and device constituent parts of device-led combination products across PMA, 510(k), and De Novo pathways. Establishes three PCCP pillars—Description of Modifications, Modification Protocol (data management/sequestration, re-training, performance evaluation, update procedures/post-market surveillance), and Impact Assessment—plus QSR compliance, labeling/UDI updates, public summary transparency, Appendix A detailed protocol questions, and Appendix B six clinical scenarios.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: FDA's AI-DSF Predetermined Change Control Plan guidance is dominantly framed around consumer_public_safety, anchoring premarket authorization, sequestered validation testing, quality-system compliance, user labeling, and post-market adverse-event monitoring in ensuring a reasonable assurance of medical device safety and effectiveness and preventing patient harm across clinical populations. Consumer_public_safety clearly leads innovation_enablement because every modification boundary and verification gate exists to preserve clinical safety and prevent injury. Innovation_enablement is a major secondary frame—adopting a 'least burdensome', forward-thinking regulatory pathway so manufacturers can iteratively improve AI medical devices without filing separate marketing submissions for every update—while fundamental_rights appears substantively through demographic representativeness, intersectional subpopulation testing, bias mitigation against historical healthcare inequalities, and human-subject clinical protections.

documents.title: From Principles to Practice | OSTP | The White House
documents.implementation_notes: Companion HTML overview page (October 2022, subsequently archived/superseded) introducing the 'From Principles to Practice' technical companion to OSTP's Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights. Explains the companion's three-part structure per principle ('Why this principle is important', 'What should be expected of automated systems', and 'How these principles can move into practice') and outlines voluntary expectations for pre-deployment testing, ongoing monitoring, governance, and public or oversight-body reporting without creating legally binding obligations.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: OSTP's 'From Principles to Practice' companion overview is dominantly framed around fundamental_rights, explicitly centering on protecting the rights, opportunities, access, privacy, and civil liberties of the American public in the design and deployment of automated systems. Fundamental_rights strongly outweighs consumer_public_safety because every section anchors technical practices and reporting in safeguarding individual rights and civil liberties rather than product reliability alone. Consumer_public_safety serves as a clear secondary frame via the stated goal of guarding the public against potential and actual harms from automated systems, with a minor innovation_enablement note on tailoring standards to specific sectors and contexts.

documents.title: Combatting Online Harms Through Innovation: A Report to Congress
documents.implementation_notes: Submitted June 16, 2022 by the FTC Bureau of Consumer Protection pursuant to Pub. L. No. 116-260, Title XV, § 1501(j). Evaluates automated and AI-based tools across seven Congressionally designated online harm categories (scams/fraud, deepfakes/fake reviews/bots, dark patterns, illegal content including opioids/CSAM/revenge porn/hate crimes/harassment/violence, terrorist and violent extremist content, election disinformation, and counterfeits). Concludes that AI detection tools remain rudimentary, brittle, context-blind, prone to bias/discrimination/overblocking, and incentivize commercial surveillance. Recommends against laws mandating AI content-filtering, and instead calls for human oversight with moderator protections, meaningful transparency/explainability/contestability, researcher access with privacy safeguards, certified independent audits and standardized Algorithmic Impact Assessments, whistleblower protections, responsible data science and documentation, content provenance/authentication (e.g., C2PA), user control tools, and transparency/accountability legislation.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The FTC Report to Congress is dominantly framed around fundamental_rights, warning that automated content-moderation tools remain rudimentary and can exacerbate algorithmic bias and discrimination against marginalized communities, chill First Amendment protected speech through overblocking, incentivize invasive commercial surveillance eroding user privacy, and deprive affected individuals of due process, explainability, contestability, and redress. Fundamental_rights narrowly edges out consumer_public_safety because while the report surveys severe online consumer harms, the FTC's core governance argument in the Executive Summary and Recommendations centers on rights-based transparency, accountability, non-discrimination, privacy, and free-speech guardrails against over-reliance on AI filtering. Consumer_public_safety is a close runner-up covering online scams, deceptive dark patterns, fake reviews, counterfeits, opioids, CSAM, revenge porn, and harassment, supported by social_stability (election disinformation, violent extremism, public trust, and the 'Liar's Dividend') and a minor national_security thread (foreign influence operations and counterterrorism).

documents.title: HHS / ONC HTI-1 Final Rule: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability — Certification Program Updates, Algorithm Transparency, and Information Sharing (89 FR 1192)
documents.issuing_body: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS / ONC)
documents.implementation_notes: Published January 9, 2024 (89 FR 1192) and effective February 8, 2024 under the HITECH Act and 21st Century Cures Act. Establishes the first binding U.S. federal regulation setting algorithm transparency and AI risk management obligations for clinical and operational healthcare AI/ML ('Predictive Decision Support Interventions' in 45 CFR § 170.102, explicitly encompassing supervised, semi-supervised, and self-supervised models including LLMs and generative AI, while excluding purely unsupervised similarity models). Replaces legacy CDS (§ 170.315(a)(9)) with DSI (§ 170.315(b)(11)) in the Base EHR definition starting January 1, 2025, requiring: (1) structured 'source attributes' (31+ metadata fields functioning as clinical model nutrition labels covering intended use, out-of-scope cautions, training data criteria and demographic/SDOH/health-status representativeness, fairness approaches, external/local validation, quantitative performance, and update schedules); (2) Intervention Risk Management (IRM) practices covering NIST AI RMF-aligned risk analysis across eight characteristics (validity, reliability, robustness, fairness, intelligibility, safety, security, privacy), risk mitigation, and data governance for all developer-supplied Predictive DSIs; (3) public hyperlink disclosure of IRM summary practices via ONC-ACBs on CHPL (§ 170.523(f)(1)(xxi)); (4) ongoing Assurances Maintenance of Certification review/updates (§ 170.402(b)(4)) and annual Real World Testing (§ 170.405); and (5) complementary interoperability, USCDI v3, SMART App Launch 2.0 / 1-hour API revocation, Insights Condition reporting (§ 170.407), and Part 171 Information Blocking / TEFCA Manner Exception rules.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The HHS/ONC HTI-1 Final Rule is dominantly framed around consumer and public safety, grounding its Predictive Decision Support Intervention transparency, risk-management, and interoperability mandates in protecting patients from clinical harm, reducing medical errors, improving sepsis and care outcomes, and ensuring healthcare AI tools are fair, appropriate, valid, effective, and safe. Fundamental rights forms a deeply intertwined secondary frame anchored in advancing 'health equity by design,' rooting out algorithmic bias and discrimination against historically underserved and marginalized communities (implementing Executive Orders 13985 and 14091), and strengthening patient data privacy, access, and authorization-revocation rights. Innovation enablement plays a major supporting role: ONC calibrates transparency guardrails without rigid performance thresholds to build public trust, unlock wider adoption of promising clinical AI tools, and foster a vibrant standards-based FHIR application ecosystem. Economic competitiveness serves as a distinct supporting frame tied to Executive Order 14036, curbing information blocking and market consolidation while correcting information asymmetry so healthcare markets reward higher-quality predictive models.

documents.title: Joint Statement on Enforcement Efforts Against Discrimination and Bias in Automated Systems
documents.implementation_notes: Issued April 25, 2023 jointly by the heads of CFPB, DOJ Civil Rights Division, EEOC, and FTC. Clarifies that established federal laws—including the FTC Act, Fair Housing Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, Title VII and other EEOC statutes, and federal consumer financial/adverse-action laws—apply fully to automated systems and AI across employment, housing, credit, education, criminal justice, voting, and consumer markets. Identifies three core risk vectors: biased/unrepresentative datasets, model opacity ('black boxes'), and flawed design/contextual assumptions. Expressly notes it is informational and not final agency action.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The Joint Statement is dominantly framed around fundamental_rights, anchoring interagency AI enforcement in core federal commitments to fairness, equality, justice, civil rights, equal opportunity, and preventing unlawful discrimination across protected classes in jobs, housing, credit, education, voting, and criminal justice. Fundamental_rights clearly edges out consumer_public_safety because anti-discrimination and equal rights form the central organizing theme across all four agencies and all three identified failure modes. Consumer_public_safety is a strong secondary frame through FTC and CFPB mandates protecting consumers from unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices, unsubstantiated claims, and invasive commercial surveillance, while innovation_enablement appears briefly to affirm that responsible innovation and adherence to law complement each other.

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Final publication of NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0, released January 26, 2023; supersedes the August 18, 2022 Second Draft). Directed by the National AI Initiative Act of 2020 (P.L. 116-283), it establishes a voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific, law- and regulation-agnostic lifecycle risk management standard structured around seven trustworthiness characteristics and four Core functions (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) with 19 categories and 72 subcategories, plus Use-Case, Temporal, and Cross-Sectoral Profiles and Appendices A–D. Planned formal community review no later than 2028.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: NIST AI RMF 1.0 is dominantly framed around innovation_enablement, presenting a voluntary, flexible, non-prescriptive, and pro-innovation framework designed to help organizations unleash AI benefits and foster trustworthy adoption across all sectors. Innovation_enablement narrowly edges out consumer_public_safety, which is a strong runner-up centered on preventing physical injury, death, property, environmental, and operational harms across the AI lifecycle. Fundamental_rights is a major third frame explicitly anchored in a 'rights-preserving' mandate, threats to civil liberties and human rights, human autonomy and dignity in privacy, and mitigation of harmful bias and discrimination, alongside minor nods to inclusive economic growth, public trust, catastrophic risk cessation, and NSCAI recommendations.

documents.title: NIST AI RMF Playbook
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Full 147-page NIST AI RMF Playbook PDF (initial catalog date 2022-07-08; full living document aligned to AI RMF 1.0 and updated through 2024). Provides voluntary, non-checklist operational guidance across all 72 subcategories of GOVERN (1.1–6.2), MANAGE (1.1–4.3), MAP (1.1–5.2), and MEASURE (1.1–4.3), supplying 'About' narratives, actionable 'Suggested Actions', 'Transparency & Documentation' self-assessment questions, 'AI Transparency Resources' (GAO-21-519SP, IC AI Ethics Framework, WEF, ALTAI, Datasheets), software toolkits, and scholarly/standards references.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The NIST AI RMF Playbook is dominantly framed around consumer_public_safety, operationalizing a 'safety-first mindset' and 'preventing harm by design and default' across 72 tactical subcategories that prioritize physical safety, protecting human life, health, property, and the environment, safeguarding minors, and preventing system failures, drift, and adversarial compromise. Consumer_public_safety edges out fundamental_rights, which is a strong runner-up woven throughout bias/fairness, disability inclusion, informed consent, privacy as human autonomy and dignity, and recourse for impacted communities. Innovation_enablement is a prominent third frame via its voluntary, selective, non-checklist design that balances trustworthiness tradeoffs with business value and trustworthy deployment, complemented by social_stability (public trust), economic prosperity, and minor national_security references.

documents.title: NIST CAISI / SI Agent Standards Initiative
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Launched in February 2026 by NIST / Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in collaboration with NCCoE and NSF (under the post-EO 14434 'Super Intelligence (SI)' portal nomenclature). This overview establishes a voluntary, industry-led standardization program for autonomous AI/SI agents centered on interoperable open protocols, agent identity, authentication, authorization, open-source ecosystem security, and security evaluations, with stakeholder consultation milestones in March–April 2026 and no regulatory mandates.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The NIST CAISI SI Agent Standards Initiative is dominantly framed around innovation_enablement, seeking to catalyze widespread, confident adoption of autonomous agents through voluntary industry-led standards, open interoperable protocols, and sector-specific barrier reduction in healthcare, finance, and education. Innovation_enablement edges out economic_competitiveness because the operational pillars center on reducing ecosystem friction and building interoperable voluntary standards rather than zero-sum trade competition. Economic_competitiveness is a notable secondary frame via explicit goals of cementing U.S. dominance at the technological frontier and maintaining international standards leadership, while consumer_public_safety appears through secure human-agent interactions, agent threat mitigations, and security evaluations for consumer comparison.

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: NIST AI 600-1 (approved July 25, 2024; published July 26, 2024), a voluntary cross-sectoral AI RMF 1.0 profile for Generative AI developed pursuant to Section 4.1(a)(i)(A) of EO 14110 and the NIST Generative AI Public Working Group (GAI PWG). Defines 12 risks unique to or exacerbated by GAI (CBRN, Confabulation, Dangerous/Violent/Hateful Content, Data Privacy, Environmental Impacts, Harmful Bias/Homogenization, Human-AI Configuration, Information Integrity, Information Security, Intellectual Property, Obscene/Degrading/Abusive Content including CSAM/NCII, and Value Chain/Component Integration) and maps ~190 suggested actions across GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE organized around Governance, Pre-Deployment Testing, Content Provenance, and Incident Disclosure (including recommended internal bans/filters against CSAM/NCII and coverage of both proprietary and open-source GAI tools).
documents.framing_rationale_summary: NIST AI 600-1 is dominantly framed around consumer_public_safety: its 12-risk taxonomy and action tables center on preventing tangible, empirically evidenced harms to users, patients, children, and the public—including confabulated medical or legal guidance, CSAM and NCII abuse, self-harm and violent instructions, offensive cyber vulnerabilities, and psychological harms from anthropomorphization and emotional entanglement. Consumer_public_safety leads fundamental_rights, which is a strong runner-up anchored in data privacy/PII leakage, systemic bias and discrimination against protected groups, intellectual property, and civil rights violations. Social_stability (information integrity, large-scale disinformation eroding public trust and democratic institutions), existential_catastrophic (CBRN weapons/BDTs, offensive cyber, halting unacceptable large-scale risks), and innovation_enablement (voluntary flexible standards to realize commercial and societal benefits) form substantial secondary frames.

documents.title: NIST IR 8596 (Initial Preliminary Draft): Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence (Cyber AI Profile)
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Initial Preliminary Draft of NIST IR 8596 (Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence / Cyber AI Profile), published December 16, 2025 for public comment through January 30, 2026 (quarantined as draft_consultation until final publication). Maps all 106 NIST CSF 2.0 Subcategories across GOVERN, IDENTIFY, PROTECT, DETECT, RESPOND, and RECOVER into three Focus Areas: Securing AI System Components (Secure), Conducting AI-Enabled Cyber Defense (Defend), and Thwarting AI-Enabled Cyber Attacks (Thwart), with Priority 1–3 ratings and detailed controls for agentic AI identity, least-privilege scoping, code-execution sandboxing, and autonomy kill-switches. Complements the NIST AI RMF and forthcoming SP 800-53 Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems (COSAiS).
documents.framing_rationale_summary: NIST IR 8596 (Cyber AI Profile) is dominantly framed around consumer_public_safety, centering on operational system resilience and protecting organizations, infrastructure (such as power grids and OT/ICS), and users from AI-related failures, data leakage, poisoning, prompt injection, deepfake phishing, and AI-accelerated cyberattacks. Consumer_public_safety narrowly edges out innovation_enablement, which is a strong runner-up emphasizing adaptable, voluntary, technology-neutral guidance that enables organizations to strategically adopt AI and capitalize on AI-enabled cyber defense efficiencies. National_security serves as a clear third frame through explicit attention to advanced persistent threats (APTs), offensive cyber operations, autonomous attack agents, AI-orchestrated espionage, and critical infrastructure resilience, with minor supporting roles for economic welfare, privacy/civil liberties compliance, and machine-speed autonomous cyber risks.

documents.title: M-25-21: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust
documents.implementation_notes: Issued April 3, 2025 by OMB Director Russell T. Vought pursuant to EO 14179, the AI in Government Act of 2020, and the Advancing American AI Act, rescinding and replacing OMB Memorandum M-24-10. Applies across executive agencies and independent regulatory agencies (excluding National Security Systems, with Intelligence Community carve-outs). Combines pro-innovation mandates (public AI strategies, mandatory government-wide sharing of custom-developed AI models/weights and open-source code release with 4 carve-outs, delegated risk acceptance) with binding governance structures (CAIOs, AI Governance Boards, CAIO Council) and 7 mandatory minimum risk management practices for 'high-impact AI' across 15 presumed high-impact categories (pre-deployment testing, AI Impact Assessments with internal independent review, ongoing monitoring, operator training, human oversight/fail-safes, human appeals/remedies, and public consultation).
documents.framing_rationale_summary: OMB Memorandum M-25-21 is dominantly framed around innovation_enablement, directing agencies to adopt a forward-leaning pro-innovation posture, cut bureaucratic bottlenecks, delegate risk acceptance, share code/models/data, and apply risk-proportionate governance as an enabler of accelerated public-sector AI adoption. Innovation_enablement edges out fundamental_rights because the overhaul replacing M-24-10 explicitly elevates barrier removal, AI maturity, and agile federal deployment as its lead organizing priority. Fundamental_rights is a strong secondary frame protecting civil rights, civil liberties, privacy, non-discrimination, protected speech, and human appeal rights across high-impact agency decisions; consumer_public_safety is prominent in ensuring safe, secure, resilient AI and fail-safes across safety-critical infrastructure, healthcare, robotics, and hazardous agents; and economic_competitiveness appears via EO 14179 global AI dominance, Buy American procurement, and taxpayer value.

documents.title: M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government
documents.implementation_notes: Issued April 3, 2025 by OMB Director Russell T. Vought pursuant to the Advancing American AI Act and EO 14179, rescinding and replacing OMB Memorandum M-24-18. Establishes binding acquisition lifecycle governance for civilian executive agencies (excluding Intelligence Community elements, National Security Systems, and common commercial products with embedded ancillary AI), pairing pro-competition anti-lock-in and Buy American AI policies with mandatory privacy/PII safeguards, data-ownership protections, proposal testing, independent agency evaluation rights, M-25-21 high-impact risk clauses, and FISMA Authorization to Operate compliance.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: OMB Memorandum M-25-22 is dominantly framed around innovation_enablement, seeking to accelerate efficient, cost-effective federal adoption of state-of-the-art AI capabilities through agile cross-functional acquisition, performance-based contracting, interoperability, and streamlined onboarding of novel vendors. Innovation_enablement edges out economic_competitiveness because the operational core focuses on modernizing public-sector acquisition workflows and enabling timely government utilization rather than external trade rivalry. Economic_competitiveness is a strong secondary frame through fostering a competitive American AI marketplace, preventing vendor lock-in, safeguarding taxpayer dollars, and maximizing Buy American AI; fundamental_rights is prominent via explicit obligations to mitigate privacy, civil rights, and civil liberties risks across the acquisition lifecycle, alongside consumer_public_safety in ensuring procured systems are safe, secure, fit for purpose, and protective of public safety.

documents.title: Roadmap for the NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) | NIST
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Companion NIST Roadmap outlining ten priority collaborative workstreams to advance AI RMF 1.0: international standards alignment/crosswalks (ISO/IEC 5338, 38507, 22989, 24028, DIS 42001, NP 42005), expanded socio-technical TEVV benchmarks/testbeds, sectoral and cross-sectoral Profiles (including hiring, criminal justice, lending, and LLMs), trustworthiness tradeoff guidance, RMF effectiveness evaluation, case studies, human-AI teaming/oversight guidance, explainability/interpretability guidance, risk-tolerance methods, and multidisciplinary tutorials. All workstreams are voluntary and contingent on available resources.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The AI RMF Roadmap is dominantly framed around innovation_enablement, setting out a flexible, voluntary, internationally aligned program of standards crosswalks, TEVV tools, profiles, case studies, and tutorials to close knowledge gaps and equip organizations to deploy trustworthy AI. Innovation_enablement leads consumer_public_safety, which is a strong secondary frame focused on reducing real-world negative impacts and harms to individuals, groups, communities, and society via TEVV, risk tolerances, and human-AI oversight. Fundamental_rights appears as a secondary rationale through the explicit 'rights-preserving' orientation and sectoral profile priorities covering hiring, criminal justice, and lending.

documents.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act (Public Law 119-12, 139 Stat. 55)
documents.implementation_notes: Public Law 119-12 (139 Stat. 55), approved May 19, 2025. First binding U.S. federal statute targeting AI-generated nonconsensual intimate visual depictions ('digital forgeries') alongside authentic NCII. Section 2 amends Section 223 of the Communications Act of 1934 to create federal criminal offenses; Section 3 mandates a covered-platform notice-and-takedown regime within 1 year (by May 19, 2026) requiring 48-hour removal and reasonable efforts to remove known identical copies, backed by good-faith takedown liability immunity and FTC UDAP rule-violation enforcement. Excludes broadband ISPs, email, and primarily non-UGC preselected-content services.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The TAKE IT DOWN Act is dominantly framed around consumer_public_safety, targeting exploitation, abuse, harassment, extortion, and concrete psychological, financial, and reputational harm to individuals—with heightened protection for minors—through federal criminalization and FTC unfair-and-deceptive-practices platform takedown enforcement. Consumer_public_safety edges out fundamental_rights because the statute anchors liability in tangible victim harm, child protection, anti-extortion, and consumer-protection UDAP enforcement rather than constitutional-rights declarations. Fundamental_rights is a strong secondary frame grounded in affirmative voluntary consent, reasonable expectations of personal privacy, and free-expression carve-outs for matters of public concern.

documents.title: Technical Contributions to AI Governance | NIST
documents.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
documents.implementation_notes: Brief NIST ITL AI Program informational overview (originally published 2021-07-26 and later updated to reference the 2023 G7 Hiroshima Process) summarizing NIST's role as a neutral technical convener, federal AI standards coordinator, and interagency/international AI governance participant. Contains no operative compliance requirements or enforcement hooks.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: This short institutional overview has sparse explicit rationale language, centered primarily on innovation_enablement: grounding domestic and international AI governance in scientific and technical realities through neutral convening, federal standards coordination, and shared research infrastructure (NAIRR) to shape effective AI development. Consumer_public_safety appears modestly via the goal of 'effective and reliable AI,' and economic_competitiveness plays a minor role through partnerships with the International Trade Administration in international governance.

documents.title: Managing Artificial Intelligence-Specific Cybersecurity Risks in the Financial Services Sector
documents.implementation_notes: Issued March 27, 2024 pursuant to Executive Order 14110 (150-day mandate) based on 42 stakeholder interviews and an annexed FSSCC R&D Committee white paper. Maps AI-specific cybersecurity and fraud threats (social engineering, malware generation, data poisoning, inference leakage, evasion, model extraction, deepfake identity impersonation, synthetic identity fraud, and third-/fourth-party supply chain risks) to existing U.S. financial supervisory frameworks and NIST AI RMF/CSF controls. Proposes ten follow-on workstreams including a common AI lexicon, narrowing the fraud-data divide for smaller institutions, expanding NIST AI RMF into a financial-sector profile with USAISI, exploring AI data supply-chain 'nutrition labels', black-box explainability R&D, workforce training, digital identity standards, and FSB/OECD/G7 international coordination.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: Treasury's report is dominantly framed around consumer and public safety, centering on protecting financial institutions, their personnel, and consumers from escalating cyber-enabled fraud, deepfake identity impersonation, synthetic identity theft, data poisoning, and operational IT disruptions. Innovation enablement serves as a strong secondary rationale: Treasury stresses the importance of prudent technological innovation, flexible non-prescriptive guidance, and public-private collaboration to help firms of all sizes safely adopt AI tools for cyber defense and anti-fraud operations. National security is a meaningful secondary frame rooted in protecting the financial services critical infrastructure sector against sophisticated cyberthreat and nation-state actors, alongside anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing resilience. Fundamental rights appears as a supporting secondary concern, highlighting consumer privacy, data protection, fairness, and the risk that financial AI systems could perpetuate or amplify inequities against historically marginalized groups.
